messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus Chen

Marcus Chen had been captain of the *Pacific Star* for sixteen years, a 280-foot container vessel that ran regular routes between Long Beach and Shanghai. He loved the ocean, loved the clarity of command, the weight of responsibility that came with knowing four hundred million dollars of cargo and a crew of twenty depended on his decisions. That love ended on a Tuesday afternoon in March when a disgruntled former crew member, turned away at the gangway, returned with a pipe bomb. The device detonated near the bridge during afternoon watch, killing two of Marcus's officers instantly and shattering the windows of the wheelhouse. Marcus himself was thrown backward, his shoulder dislocated, his hearing temporarily gone. What stayed with him longer than the physical injuries was the moment just before the explosion—a sound like a door slamming, then nothing, then the world tilting sideways. The man who planted the bomb was arrested within hours. He served four years and was released two years ago on a legal technicality. Marcus read about it in a maritime newsletter. No one had asked Marcus's opinion. No one seemed to think it mattered.

In the months after the blast, Marcus had tried to return to work. His company offered him a shore-based position—administrative, safe, landlocked. He refused it. He was a ship's captain; the sea was his life. But within weeks of resuming command, he found himself unable to trust his crew. They were competent, loyal, many of them the same men who'd been aboard that day, yet Marcus had come to believe he could not rely on other people, not really, not when it mattered. Someone could always turn on you. Someone could walk away one day and return with violence. This certainty had hardened into something unshakeable. The thought that he might be wrong, that he might be able to trust again, felt impossibly dangerous—if he lowered his guard and someone hurt his crew, he would not survive it. Better to assume the worst and be ready.

That assumption began to reshape his days. Marcus found himself hypervigilant for dangerous people on the dock, studying the faces of vendors and port officials with an intensity that made others uncomfortable. He started choosing which crew members could access the bridge, which could be near the fuel lines. He positioned himself always with his back to a wall, always able to see the exits. When they were in port, he would not leave the ship. When he had to be ashore, he avoided unfamiliar places entirely—he could not assess the danger in new territory, could not control the variables, and the uncertainty itself felt like a threat. His wife, Sarah, asked him to attend her company holiday party in a hotel ballroom downtown. He declined. He chose a table at the back of restaurants, never the center, never anywhere he felt exposed. At night, he lay awake beside Sarah, unable to fall asleep because he needed to stay alert, to listen for sounds that didn't belong, to keep watch. His mind would race through scenarios: a fire at the dock, an intruder on deck, an accident he hadn't foreseen. Sleep felt like surrender.

Within six months, Marcus had given up the shore-based administrative role he'd briefly accepted—a decision that baffled his company, but he couldn't bear being in an office where he couldn't see the exits, couldn't monitor the hallways. He dropped his involvement in the maritime union's safety committee, a position he'd held proudly for a decade. He stopped attending his daughter's soccer games because the field was too open, too exposed, and he couldn't position himself safely. Each responsibility he shed felt necessary, a calculation of risk versus safety, yet each one also confirmed his deepest fear: that he was becoming someone unreliable, someone who couldn't show up for the people who needed him. That fear fed his sense that others couldn't rely on him either, which made his conviction that he couldn't rely on them feel even more justified. If he was failing them, surely they would fail him.

To manage the creeping dread, Marcus began gambling. A casino forty minutes from home became a place he could go—enclosed, controlled, with clear exits and security cameras he could see. The noise and stimulation there distracted him from the constant scanning, the endless vigilance. He told Sarah it was a stress release, a way to unwind, but it was more than that. It was permission to stop thinking, to let his mind go blank in the rush of placing bets and watching the reels spin. He lost seven thousand dollars in three months. When Sarah found the credit card statements, she wept. He couldn't explain it in a way that made sense to her, couldn't articulate that the gambling was the only time he didn't feel like he was failing everyone, the only time he could escape the loop of hypervigilance and shame.

Then, last month, a police officer came aboard during a routine port inspection. His uniform—navy blue, badge, the weight of authority—triggered something visceral in Marcus. He found himself unable to stay in the room. He left the bridge, his hands shaking, his breath shallow. Later, when a container fell on the dock and made a sound like an explosion, Marcus flinched so violently he nearly fell. His crew noticed. Word would get back to the company. He was unraveling, and he knew it.

What frightened Marcus most now was the thought that if he allowed himself to think about the bombing, to really think about it, he would not be able to handle it—that he would fall apart entirely and there would be no coming back. So he didn't think about it. He pushed it away, kept moving, kept scanning, kept gambling, kept avoiding. But the avoidance was becoming its own trap. He was missing his life. Sarah had stopped asking him to come home early. His daughter had stopped inviting him to games. And somewhere in that silence, Marcus had begun to wonder if the man who planted the bomb had already won—not with the explosion, but with this: the slow erosion of everything that made him who he was. It was this thought, finally, that made him call a therapist. He needed to know if there was any way back, or if he was truly alone in this, as he had come to believe.
